The study used a high-frequency induction furnace with a maximum melting capacity of 300 kg to re-melt and balance the composition of steel scrap.
The targeted 17-4 PH stainless steel composition was achieved by adding Ferro-alloy components such as Ni, Cr, Mo, Cu, and Nb during the balancing process.
The investment casting mold was designed to have a wall thickness less than 0.5 mm to accommodate the solidification rate of the martensitic-type stainless steel.
X-ray radiography of the turbine blade prototypes showed acceptable quality with no major defects such as porosity, cracks, or inclusions.
The as-cast scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel had a tensile strength of 676.74 MPa and elongation of 9.33%.
Aging the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel at 580°C for 2 hours after austenitizing at 1050°C resulted in a yield strength of 894.17 MPa and elongation of 3.45%.
The microstructure of the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel consisted of a martensitic matrix with the presence of delta ferrite and precipitation of intermetallic phases such as carbides.
The addition of niobium was found to assist in the formation of intermetallic precipitates, which act as nucleation sites and help lower the elastic deformation energy during precipitation hardening.

Geothermal power plants typically use martensitic stainless steels like AISI 410 and 420 for turbine blades, while the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel offers an alternative with improved corrosion resistance and precipitation hardening.

The scrap-based approach using induction melting and investment casting can provide a more cost-effective and sustainable method of manufacturing turbine components, especially in regions with limited domestic stainless steel production.
The study did not evaluate the corrosion resistance properties of the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel against geothermal fluids, as this was outside the scope of the current investigation.

The investment casting process used in this study was practiced in a smaller setup at a local manufacturer, with similar steps and conditions used for casting stainless steel products in their production line.
The study used a combination of Kalling's no.2 etchant and Murakami's reagent to reveal the martensitic structure, delta ferrite, and secondary phases in the microstructural analysis.
The commercial 17-4 PH stainless steel product used as a reference had a tensile strength of 1070 MPa and elongation of 16%.

The study found that the scrap-based 17-4 PH stainless steel can be a viable option for manufacturing turbine blades in geothermal power plants, with the potential for cost and sustainability benefits.
